nameStory: The red-winged blackbird gets its name from the male's striking scarlet shoulder patches, called 'epaulets,' that flash brilliantly when he spreads his wings or displays his territory. These bright red badges stand out like military insignia against his jet-black feathers, making him impossible to miss during breeding season.
description: Red-winged blackbirds are medium-sized songbirds about the size of a robin, with males and females looking completely different from each other. Males are glossy black all over with bright red shoulder patches bordered by yellow, while females are streaky brown and often mistaken for large sparrows. They're one of the most common birds in North America, with massive flocks that can contain millions of individuals during winter.

idTips.label: Male's red shoulder patches
idTips.description: Brilliant scarlet patches on the shoulders that flash like stop signs when the bird flies or displays, often bordered by a thin yellow stripe that catches the light

idTips.label: Female's streaky brown plumage
idTips.description: Heavily streaked brown and buff coloring that looks like someone took a paintbrush and striped her from head to tail, with a slightly pointed bill

idTips.label: Male's conk-la-ree call
idTips.description: A liquid, gurgling song that sounds like 'conk-la-ree' or 'oak-a-lee,' often delivered while perched prominently on cattails or fence posts

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Males love to perch conspicuously on tall marsh plants, fence posts, or phone wires with their red patches displayed, while females skulk lower in vegetation

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Undulating flight with alternating flaps and glides, red patches flashing on and off like turn signals as the wings beat

habitat: Red-winged blackbirds love wetlands and marshy areas throughout New England, especially cattail marshes, pond edges, and roadside ditches. You'll also find them in wet meadows, agricultural fields near water, and even parking lot storm drains with standing water. They need some water nearby but will forage in dry fields and suburban areas during non-breeding seasons.

seasonality.spring: Males arrive first in March, setting up territories and singing constantly from prominent perches, their red patches blazing as they chase rivals and court the more secretive females who arrive later.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season with males aggressively defending territories while females build cup-shaped nests hidden in cattails or shrubs, often raising 2-3 broods.
seasonality.fall: Family groups join together into increasingly large flocks that roam fields and marshes, with males' red patches less prominent as they focus on feeding.
seasonality.winter: Many migrate south, but some remain in New England, forming massive mixed flocks with other blackbirds that can darken the sky when they take flight.

funFact: Red-winged blackbird flocks can be so enormous that a single winter roost has been recorded containing over 15 million birds - that's enough blackbirds to give every person in New England two birds each, with millions left over!
confusionNotes: Female red-winged blackbirds are often confused with large sparrows or female house finches due to their brown, streaky appearance. Look for the red-wing's longer, more pointed bill and slightly larger size - plus you'll usually spot a flashy male nearby defending territory during breeding season.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name suggesting they're blackbirds, red-winged blackbirds aren't closely related to European blackbirds at all - they're actually part of the New World blackbird family that includes orioles, meadowlarks, and grackles. The family name Icteridae comes from the Greek word for 'jaundice' because many species have bright yellow coloring.
compareHints: Red-winged blackbirds are the only members of their genus in New England, but they can be compared to other blackbirds in the region. Male red-wings are smaller and sleeker than common grackles (which have longer tails and iridescent purple-green heads), and lack the rusty breast of male rusty blackbirds. No other blackbird species has those distinctive red shoulder patches.
